findings.F1: Every coin drifts up in the late UTC evening, whatever its past 24 hours did. Hourly returns on bars closing at 21:00 and 22:00 UTC average +5.45bp (t 6.75, n 17403) and +4.36bp (t 5.66, n 17417); no other hour exceeds |t| 3.8. Over those two hours each coin averages +4.2 to +5.5bp (t 3.0 to 4.4), every weekday is positive (t 2.1 to 3.9), 7 of 8 years are positive (2022 is -2.2bp, t -1.4), and 83% of windows have a positive mean.
findings.F2: The book cannot turn the confirmed 2-hour edge into money. Its 7238 trades last 1.0 hour on median and lose 0.095% before fees (t -7.2) and 0.195% after; every coin is negative after fees (-0.11% to -0.27%). The position held over the bar closing at 21:00 gains only +1.87bp (t 2.38, n 7225), the second positive hour (22:00) is not held, and the round-trip fee of about 0.10% is larger than either.
findings.F3: Over a day, a large fall measured against the coin's own volatility is followed by a rebound. On a non-overlapping 24-hour grid, the 24-hour return in units of 30-day volatility has its lowest decile followed by +81.8bp excess over the next 24 hours (t 5.21, n 1596) and its second decile by +29.3bp (t 2.30); deciles 3 to 10 lie between -24 and -4bp. The slope is negative in all 6 coins (t -2.3 to -4.4) and in 7 of 8 years (t +0.54 in 2024).

ideas.idea: A coin rises over the 2 hours after the 20:00 UTC close, and the rise is larger the larger the coin's average absolute hourly return over its past 30 days.
ideas.consequence: A trader would hold, or refuse to short, a coin through the 21–22 UTC hours and expect more from the more volatile coins.
ideas.name: late-evening drift scaled by volatility

ideas.idea: The larger a coin's fall over its past 24 hours, measured in units of its own 30-day volatility, the more the coin rises over the next 24 hours.
ideas.consequence: A trader would buy, or refuse to short, a coin after a fall that is large for that coin, and hold it for about a day rather than a few hours.
ideas.name: volatility-scaled daily fall rebound

ideas.idea: After a 24-hour fall, the higher the coin's 24-hour volatility relative to its 30-day volatility, the more the coin rises over the next 24 hours.
ideas.consequence: A trader would favour buying falls that came with a burst of turbulence, and refuse to short them, for a one-day rebound.
ideas.name: turbulent falls rebound harder

ideas.idea: After a 24-hour fall, the more evenly the fall is spread across its hours (the smaller its largest single hour's share of the hourly moves), the more the coin rises over the next 24 hours.
ideas.consequence: A trader would expect a day-long rebound after broad, many-hour selloffs, and refuse to short them, more than after falls made in a single hour.
ideas.name: spread-out falls rebound more
